name: Percentage Error
description: Learn about Percentage Error and its applications in physics.

content.overview: "My experiment was off by 2%." Ever notice how much more sense that makes than "my experiment was off by 0.4 grams"? That's the whole point of percentage error—it's just relative error dressed up as a percentage so everyone instantly gets how big the mistake really was. {{viz:diagram-01}}
keyPoints: Percentage error = relative error × 100 = (absolute error ÷ true value) × 100 {{viz:diagram-02}}
It's the human-friendly way to express how big an error really is
A percentage error under about 5% is usually considered solid for a hands-on physics experiment
Same paperclip example: 50% error. Same running track: 0.01% error
content.whyItMatters: Whenever you read a lab report, a product spec sheet, or a news article about a measurement, percentage error is usually the number quoted. It's the universal language for "how good was this measurement, really?"—way more intuitive than a raw decimal fraction.
